The correct response: (1) create a standard risk response that every PM can use (template), (2) potentially address the root cause at the supply chain level (dual sourcing, safety stock, better supplier qualification). Simply adding it to future risk registers without a standard response repeats the reactive pattern. Blaming procurement without root cause analysis is scapegoating.
source: CAPM ECO 2023 - Domain 1 T2 / Lessons Learned / OPA Development

question: A BA is eliciting requirements from a group of end users. During a workshop, a senior manager in the room consistently overrides the end users' stated needs with their own preferences. The end users stop contributing. What technique should the BA use to recover the session?
options: A. Ask the senior manager to leave the workshop

B. Pause the workshop and schedule separate sessions — one with the senior manager and one with end users only — to elicit requirements independently, then reconcile through a structured prioritization process
C. Continue the workshop but privately ask the senior manager to hold their comments
D. Accept the senior manager's requirements as final since they have organizational authority
correct: B. Pause the workshop and schedule separate sessions — one with the senior manager and one with end users only — to elicit requirements independently, then reconcile through a structured prioritization process
explanation: A classic HiPPO (Highest Paid Person's Opinion) dynamic is killing the workshop's purpose. End user needs are being suppressed by authority, not by logic. The BA's professional responsibility is to elicit authentic needs from all relevant sources. Continuing the joint session won't change the dynamic. The solution: separate sessions to capture authentic input from each group, then use a structured reconciliation (MoSCoW, priority matrix) to surface conflicts for transparent decision-making. Asking the senior manager to leave is confrontational and politically risky. Accepting authority as a substitute for user needs will produce a system that doesn't work for those who use it.
source: CAPM ECO 2023 - Domain 4 T2/T3 / Requirements Elicitation Techniques

question: A project manager needs to estimate a software development project with 200 function points. Historical data shows the organization completes 10 function points per person-month. The team has 4 developers. How long will the project take, and what estimating technique is being used?
options: A. 5 months using Bottom-Up Estimating
B. 20 person-months total / 4 developers = 5 months, using Parametric Estimating based on the productivity rate (10 FP/person-month)
C. 50 months using Analogous Estimating from a similar project
D. 4 months using Three-Point (PERT) Estimating with optimistic assumptions
correct: B. 20 person-months total / 4 developers = 5 months, using Parametric Estimating based on the productivity rate (10 FP/person-month)
explanation: Parametric Estimating uses a statistical relationship between a parameter (function points) and historical productivity data (10 FP/person-month). Total effort = 200 FP ÷ 10 FP/person-month = 20 person-months. With 4 developers: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 months. This is textbook parametric estimating. The formula is: Estimate = Parameter × Rate. This is more accurate than analogous (which uses total project comparison) and faster than bottom-up (which requires work package decomposition). The key: parametric REQUIRES reliable historical data for the rate to be valid.
source: CAPM ECO 2023 - Domain 2 T3 / Parametric Estimating / PMBOK 7th

question: A new Scrum team has been self-organizing for 2 sprints. In Sprint 3, a senior developer starts assigning tasks to junior members without discussion, citing efficiency. Other team members begin deferring to this developer's decisions without challenge. The Scrum Master notices the team is no longer self-organizing. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: A. Allow the arrangement — the senior developer is experienced and the team seems to function smoothly

B. Raise the pattern in the Sprint Retrospective, coach the team on self-organization principles, and work with the senior developer privately to reframe their role as a technical mentor rather than a task assigner
C. Remove the senior developer's decision-making authority by establishing a formal rotation for task assignment
D. Assign tasks yourself as Scrum Master to prevent any one person from dominating
correct: B. Raise the pattern in the Sprint Retrospective, coach the team on self-organization principles, and work with the senior developer privately to reframe their role as a technical mentor rather than a task assigner
explanation: Self-organization is a core Agile principle — the team collectively decides who does what. When one person assumes a command-and-control role, the team loses the collaborative intelligence that makes Agile teams high-performing. The Scrum Master's response: (1) surface the pattern transparently in the retrospective (team awareness), (2) coach on self-organization principles, (3) private coaching for the senior developer — reframe their expertise as mentorship, not direction. Formal task assignment rotations create bureaucracy. Scrum Masters assigning tasks replaces one command-and-control dynamic with another.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 / CAPM ECO 2023 - Domain 3 T1/T5 / Agile Practice Guide

question: A project manager receives a status report showing: BAC = $1,000,000, PV = $400,000, EV = $320,000, AC = $380,000. The project is 40% complete by calendar time. A board member asks: 'Will the project finish on budget?' What is the MOST accurate response based on ALL relevant EVM indicators?
options: A. Yes — the cost variance is only -$60,000 which is manageable

B. No — CPI is 0.84, meaning for every dollar spent only $0.84 of value is earned. EAC = $1,000,000 / 0.84 = ~$1,190,000, a projected $190,000 overrun. The project is also behind schedule (SPI = 0.80) which may add further cost pressure
C. It is too early to tell — we are only 40% through the project
D. Yes — the team will improve efficiency in the second half of the project as they build momentum
correct: B. No — CPI is 0.84, meaning for every dollar spent only $0.84 of value is earned. EAC = $1,000,000 / 0.84 = ~$1,190,000, a projected $190,000 overrun. The project is also behind schedule (SPI = 0.80) which may add further cost pressure
explanation: Full EVM analysis: CPI = EV/AC = 320,000/380,000 = 0.842. SPI = EV/PV = 320,000/400,000 = 0.80. CV = EV-AC = -60,000 (over budget). SV = EV-PV = -80,000 (behind schedule). EAC = BAC/CPI = 1,000,000/0.842 = $1,187,648. The project is both over budget AND behind schedule. Being behind schedule often adds cost pressure (extended duration = more overhead, potential crashing costs). Option A only looks at CV in isolation. Option C is dismissive — 40% complete with consistent trends IS meaningful data. Option D is wishful thinking without evidence.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process T5 / Measurement Performance Domain

question: During a project, the PM observes that the team consistently avoids raising bad news in project meetings, even when problems are serious. Status reports are consistently optimistic. The PM suspects this is organizational culture, not individual dishonesty. What is the MOST effective systemic intervention?
options: A. Mandate that team members report all problems immediately or face consequences

B. Create structured 'red flag' slots in every meeting where raising concerns is explicitly valued and rewarded, model vulnerability by sharing your own uncertainties openly, and eliminate any visible negative reactions to bad news
C. Implement anonymous status reporting so team members can share problems without fear
D. Conduct individual performance reviews that measure the accuracy of status reports
correct: B. Create structured 'red flag' slots in every meeting where raising concerns is explicitly valued and rewarded, model vulnerability by sharing your own uncertainties openly, and eliminate any visible negative reactions to bad news
explanation: 'Happy path' reporting is a systemic psychological safety failure — not an individual honesty problem. The PM must address the SYSTEM: (1) Structure: create explicit space for bad news in meeting formats (a 'concerns' agenda item signals it's expected). (2) Model: the PM sharing their own uncertainties demonstrates it's safe to do so. (3) Reinforce: visibly thank people who raise hard issues — 'Thank you for flagging that early; that's exactly what we need.' (4) Never punish: any visible frustration at bad news will silence reporters immediately. Anonymous reporting treats a symptom without building culture. Mandates create compliance without psychological safety.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain I People T10/T12/T14 / Psychological Safety

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
question: A project is using a Phase Gate (Stage Gate) review process. The project has completed Phase 1 (Discovery) and is presenting to the Steering Committee for a go/no-go decision on Phase 2. The Phase 1 deliverables are complete but the business case has weakened slightly due to market changes. What criteria should drive the go/no-go decision?
options: A. Phase 1 completion — since the work was completed as planned, the project should proceed
B. Sunk cost — since $200,000 was invested in Phase 1, the project must continue to recover the investment
C. The updated business case and strategic fit — if Phase 2 still delivers sufficient value given current conditions, proceed; if not, stop or pivot regardless of Phase 1 completion or sunk costs
D. Stakeholder pressure — if key sponsors want to continue, the project should proceed
correct: C. The updated business case and strategic fit — if Phase 2 still delivers sufficient value given current conditions, proceed; if not, stop or pivot regardless of Phase 1 completion or sunk costs
explanation: Phase gate decisions are forward-looking investment decisions — not backward-looking accountability reviews. The sunk cost fallacy is one of the most common and costly decision errors in project management. The $200,000 spent on Phase 1 is gone regardless of whether Phase 2 proceeds. The only relevant question: does Phase 2 create sufficient value given current conditions? Phase 1 completion proves execution capability but doesn't justify Phase 2. Stakeholder pressure without business justification is governance failure. PMI emphasizes value-driven decision making throughout PMBOK 7th.
source: CAPM ECO 2023 - Domain 1 T4 / Business Case / Phase Gate Reviews

question: A BA is asked to document acceptance criteria for a user story: 'As a customer, I want to reset my password so that I can regain access to my account.' Which set of acceptance criteria is BEST?
options: A. 'The password reset feature works correctly'
B. 'The system sends an email' and 'The user can create a new password'

C. 'Given a registered user who has forgotten their password, when they enter their email and click Reset, then they receive a reset email within 60 seconds; the reset link expires after 24 hours; after setting a new password, the previous password no longer works; and the user is logged in automatically after resetting'
D. 'The feature passes all QA tests and is approved by the product manager'
correct: C. 'Given a registered user who has forgotten their password, when they enter their email and click Reset, then they receive a reset email within 60 seconds; the reset link expires after 24 hours; after setting a new password, the previous password no longer works; and the user is logged in automatically after resetting'
explanation: Good acceptance criteria follow the Given-When-Then (GWT) format and are SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Testable. Option C covers: (1) the trigger (user enters email), (2) expected behavior (email within 60 seconds — measurable), (3) security requirement (link expires — specific), (4) security enforcement (old password invalidated — testable), (5) UX expectation (auto login — specific). Option A is unmeasurable and untestable. Option B is incomplete. Option D defers criteria to others rather than specifying them — it's a process step, not an acceptance criterion.
source: CAPM ECO 2023 - Domain 4 T6 / Acceptance Criteria / BA for Practitioners

question: A project manager is planning a hybrid project. The regulatory compliance workstream must follow a predictive waterfall approach due to audit requirements. The product development workstream is using 2-week Agile sprints. Both workstreams share 3 developers. How should the PM address the resource contention in planning?
options: A. Separate the two workstreams completely with dedicated teams — no sharing allowed
B. Use the predictive workstream's Gantt chart as the master plan and convert all Agile sprint plans to fit within it

C. Create a hybrid integration plan: use the predictive workstream's milestones as fixed constraints in the overall roadmap, align sprint planning to avoid peak demand from compliance activities, and use resource capacity planning to model load across both workstreams with explicit buffers during compliance audit periods
D. Prioritize the compliance workstream entirely — regulatory requirements always take precedence over product development
correct: C. Create a hybrid integration plan: use the predictive workstream's milestones as fixed constraints in the overall roadmap, align sprint planning to avoid peak demand from compliance activities, and use resource capacity planning to model load across both workstreams with explicit buffers during compliance audit periods
explanation: Hybrid project management requires integrating two different approaches without forcing either into the other's mold. The solution: (1) Compliance milestones become fixed constraints — they cannot move. (2) Sprint planning is coordinated to avoid coinciding with compliance peak periods (audit prep, documentation sprints). (3) Capacity planning models both demands simultaneously and identifies crunch periods in advance. (4) Buffers protect shared resources during high-compliance periods. Converting Agile work to waterfall removes Agile's value. Full separation may not be feasible or efficient with shared resources. Always prioritizing compliance risks missing product delivery.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process T5/T6/T13 / Hybrid Project Management

question: A PM has just delivered a successful project — on time, on budget, full scope. Six months later, the PM learns that the business unit that received the deliverable has not adopted the system and is still using the old process. Benefits have not been realized. Who is responsible, and what should have been done differently?
options: A. The business unit is responsible — the PM delivered what was promised and the adoption is an operational matter
B. The PM failed — a successful project must ensure benefits are realized, not just deliverables are delivered
C. The sponsor is solely responsible for benefits realization post-delivery

D. The PM should have included a change management and adoption plan in the project scope, engaged end users throughout delivery to build readiness, and established clear benefits realization metrics with the sponsor — though post-project benefits ownership transfers to the business
D. This is an IT failure — the system was not designed to be user-friendly enough
correct: D. The PM should have included a change management and adoption plan in the project scope, engaged end users throughout delivery to build readiness, and established clear benefits realization metrics with the sponsor — though post-project benefits ownership transfers to the business
explanation: PMBOK 7th Edition explicitly addresses value delivery — a project is successful only if it generates the intended benefits, not just delivers outputs. While post-delivery benefits ownership transfers to the business, the PM has a responsibility to: (1) include organizational change management in scope, (2) engage end users early (not just at delivery), (3) establish adoption metrics and handover criteria, and (4) design the transition plan. A system that isn't adopted is a failed investment regardless of delivery metrics. The PM cannot control adoption post-handover, but can significantly influence readiness — which is a project responsibility.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain III BE T2 / PMBOK 7th - Value Delivery / Change Management
